items.value: International Monetary Fund
items.reasoning: The Rapid Financing Instrument (RFI) and the Rapid Credit Facility (RCF) are both IMF emergency lending windows: the RFI is available to all member countries facing an urgent balance-of-payments need, while the RCF is its concessional counterpart, restricted to low-income countries eligible under the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust. Both were heavily used for COVID-19 emergency disbursements. The ADB and World Bank use project loans and policy-based lending under different names, and UNEP-FI is a partnership on sustainable finance, not a lender.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — a rising NEER means the rupee is appreciating, and higher relative domestic inflation widens the NEER-REER gap; a rising REER means LOSS of competitiveness, not improvement
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: in the RBI's index convention a rise in the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate means the rupee has strengthened against the trade-weighted basket. Statement 2 is the trap and is wrong: REER is NEER adjusted for relative prices, so a rise means Indian goods have become dearer in real terms abroad — competitiveness DETERIORATES, it does not improve. Statement 3 is correct because REER equals NEER multiplied by the domestic-to-foreign price ratio; if domestic inflation runs faster than abroad, that multiplier keeps growing and the two indices diverge further.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 only — RBI sells dollars against a depreciating rupee and buys dollars when foreign rates fall; against high inflation it SELLS government securities, it does not buy them
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: buying government securities injects rupee liquidity into the system, which is expansionary and would worsen inflation; to fight high inflation the RBI conducts open market SALES to absorb liquidity. Statement 2 is correct — selling dollars adds to the supply of foreign exchange and props up the rupee. Statement 3 is correct because a fall in US or EU interest rates widens the yield differential in India's favour, pulling in capital inflows; the resulting dollar surplus would push the rupee up sharply, so the RBI buys dollars to moderate the appreciation and add to reserves.

items.value: Both statements are correct — the G20 Common Framework was endorsed jointly by the G20 and the Paris Club, and it targets low-income countries with unsustainable debt
items.reasoning: The 'Common Framework for Debt Treatments beyond the DSSI' was agreed in November 2020 by the G20 together with the Paris Club, which is precisely what makes it novel — it brought non-Paris-Club creditors such as China and India into a common debt-restructuring process. Its eligibility is tied to the Debt Service Suspension Initiative, whose beneficiaries are low-income countries, and it is meant for countries whose debt is unsustainable rather than merely illiquid. Both statements therefore hold.

items.value: Statements 1 and 2 only — IIBs let the government borrow at a lower coupon and shield investors from inflation risk, but their interest and capital gains ARE taxable
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: because the principal is indexed to inflation, the investor no longer needs an inflation-risk premium built into the coupon, so the government can issue at a lower real coupon rate. Statement 2 is correct and is the instrument's entire purpose — the investor's real return is protected whatever inflation turns out to be. Statement 3 is wrong: inflation-indexed bonds in India carry no special tax exemption; both the interest and the capital gains are taxed under the ordinary provisions, which is a recognised drawback of the instrument.

items.value: Statement 2 only — a foreign-owned e-commerce firm may not sell its own goods on its platform, but the extent to which it may own the sellers on that platform is restricted
items.reasoning: India's FDI policy permits 100% foreign investment in the marketplace model only; the inventory-based model, in which the platform owns the goods it sells, is closed to foreign investment. So statement 1 is wrong — these firms cannot sell their own goods alongside running the marketplace. Statement 2 is correct: Press Note 2 of 2018 bars a marketplace entity from selling goods of any vendor in which it (or its group companies) holds equity, and caps any single vendor at 25% of the platform's sales, which is exactly a limit on how far it can own its big sellers.

items.value: Only 1 and 2 — harvesting crops and converting cotton into fabric are real-sector activities; bank lending and issuing bonds overseas belong to the financial sector
items.reasoning: The real sector covers the actual production of goods and services, where output is physically created; the financial sector covers the movement of funds and claims. Farming (1) and manufacturing fabric from raw cotton (2) both produce goods and are unambiguously real sector. A commercial bank lending to a trading company (3) is an intermediation of funds, and a corporate issuing Rupee Denominated Bonds abroad (4) is a capital-raising transaction — both are financial-sector activities that transfer purchasing power rather than create output.

items.value: A foreign company transfers shares that derive their substantial value from assets located in India
items.reasoning: 'Indirect transfer' is the tax concept at the heart of the Vodafone and Cairn disputes: instead of selling the Indian asset directly, an offshore holding company's shares change hands, but because those shares draw their value substantially from Indian assets, India asserts the right to tax the gain under Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act. Options A, B and C all describe direct cross-border investment or a straightforward sale of foreign assets, in which no Indian underlying asset is transferred indirectly.

items.value: Statement 1 only — buying new technology is capital expenditure; debt and equity are methods of financing, not categories of expenditure at all
items.reasoning: Acquiring new technology creates an asset that yields benefits over several accounting periods, so it is capitalised rather than charged wholly against the current year's revenue — statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 confuses two different things: debt financing and equity financing are ways of raising money on the liabilities side of the balance sheet, not ways of spending it. Neither is an 'expenditure', so labelling one capital and the other revenue is meaningless.

items.value: Both statements are correct — household financial savings do finance part of government borrowing, and auctioned dated securities at market rates are a large share of internal debt
items.reasoning: Households are the principal net savers in the economy, and their savings reach the government both directly (small savings schemes, provident funds) and indirectly through banks and insurers that hold government securities under statutory and prudential requirements — so statement 1 holds. Statement 2 is also correct: dated Government of India securities, issued through competitive auctions at market-determined yields, form by far the largest single component of the Centre's internal debt.

items.value: Statements 1, 2 and 4 — the Sanyal Committee report led to the 1971 Act, Articles 129 and 215 empower the courts to punish contempt, and Parliament can legislate on contempt; but the Constitution does not define civil and criminal contempt
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the H.N. Sanyal Committee (1961) reviewed the contempt law and its recommendations produced the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. Statement 2 is correct — Article 129 makes the Supreme Court and Article 215 the High Courts courts of record with power to punish for contempt of themselves. Statement 4 is correct because Entry 77 of the Union List and Entry 14 of the Concurrent List give the legislature competence over contempt of court, which is how the 1971 Act was enacted. Statement 3 is the false one: 'civil contempt' and 'criminal contempt' are defined in Section 2 of the 1971 Act, not anywhere in the Constitution.

items.value: Statement 2 only — Bar Councils do lay down rules on legal education and recognition of law colleges, but the description of who is and is not recognised as an advocate in statement 1 is wrong
items.reasoning: Statement 2 is correct: Section 7 of the Advocates Act, 1961 charges the Bar Council of India with promoting legal education, laying down standards in consultation with the universities, and recognising universities whose law degree qualifies a person for enrolment. Statement 1 fails because the Advocates Act recognises only individual persons enrolled on a State roll — a legal FIRM cannot itself be an advocate, so the claim that legal firms are recognised as advocates is untrue, whatever the position of government law officers or corporate counsel. The judgement call is that the firm clause alone is enough to defeat the statement, which is why this is not marked HIGH.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 only — presidential assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill is obligatory and each House must pass it separately by special majority with no joint sitting; but no prior recommendation of the President is required to introduce it
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: unlike a Money Bill or a bill under Article 3, an amendment bill under Article 368 can be introduced by any member in either House without the President's prior recommendation. Statement 2 is correct — the 24th Amendment inserted into Article 368(2) the words that the President 'shall give his assent', removing any discretion. Statement 3 is correct: Article 368 requires passage in each House separately by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting, and the joint-sitting mechanism of Article 108 is expressly unavailable for constitutional amendment bills, so a deadlock simply kills the bill.

items.value: Statement 2 only — the 15% ceiling on the size of the Council of Ministers is in the Constitution, but the four-fold ranking of ministers is not
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: the Constitution nowhere classifies ministers into Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State with Independent Charge, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers — that hierarchy is a matter of convention and executive practice, and Article 74 speaks only of a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head. Statement 2 is correct: Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment Act of 2003, caps the total number of ministers including the Prime Minister at 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.

items.value: Only the no-confidence motion is exclusive to the Lok Sabha; ratifying an Emergency proclamation and impeaching the President both involve the Rajya Sabha as well
items.reasoning: A motion of no-confidence can be moved and carried only in the Lok Sabha, because Article 75(3) makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to that House alone — so statement 2 is an exclusive power. Statement 1 is not exclusive: a proclamation of Emergency must be approved by BOTH Houses within one month. Statement 3 is not exclusive either — under Article 61 the impeachment charge may be preferred by either House and is then investigated by the other, so both Houses necessarily participate.

items.value: Statement 2 only — the Tenth Schedule fixes no deadline for the presiding officer to decide a defection case; and it allows a nominated member to join a party WITHIN six months, disqualifying him only if he joins after that
items.reasoning: Statement 1 inverts the rule. Paragraph 2(3) of the Tenth Schedule disqualifies a nominated member who joins a political party AFTER the expiry of six months from taking his seat — meaning the six-month window is exactly the period in which he is permitted to join, not barred from joining. Statement 2 is correct and is the law's most criticised gap: no time limit is prescribed for the Speaker or Chairman to decide a disqualification petition, which has allowed cases to be kept pending for the life of a House and has repeatedly drawn Supreme Court comment.

items.value: Neither statement is correct — only the Attorney General, not the Solicitor General, may take part in parliamentary proceedings, and no constitutional provision requires the AG to resign when the appointing government resigns
items.reasoning: Statement 1 fails because Article 88 confers the right to speak in and take part in the proceedings of either House, its committees and any joint sitting on the Attorney General alone; the Solicitor General has no such constitutional right, so 'the only officers' is wrong on its face. Statement 2 fails on the words 'According to the Constitution': Article 76(4) says only that the Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President. The practice of tendering resignation when the appointing government goes is a healthy convention, but the Constitution does not prescribe it.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — mandamus lies against a private body only where it discharges a public duty, and any public-spirited person may seek quo warranto; but mandamus CAN lie against a government company
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the test for mandamus is the nature of the duty, so a purely private organisation is outside its reach unless the law has entrusted it with a public function. Statement 2 is wrong for the same reason — a government company that performs public duties or is an instrumentality of the State is amenable to mandamus, so a blanket exclusion of companies is untenable. Statement 3 is correct: quo warranto is an exception to the usual locus standi rule, since the wrong is the usurpation of a public office, and any member of the public may apply even without a personal grievance.

items.value: Statement 3 only — the Mission provides seamless portability of health records across the country, but participation by hospitals and by citizens is voluntary, not mandatory
items.reasoning: The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission is built on voluntary participation: creating an ABHA health account, linking records to it, and a hospital's enrolment in the health facility registry are all opt-in, so statement 1's 'must adopt' is wrong. Statement 2 fails for the same reason — the Mission supports universal health coverage as an objective, but it does not follow, and the Mission does not claim, that every citizen must ultimately be enrolled. Statement 3 is correct and is a headline feature: once records are linked to a health ID, they can be accessed and carried across providers anywhere in India. Marked MED because statement 2 rests on reading 'should be part of it' as a compulsion claim.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — the Speaker fixes the date of the Deputy Speaker's election and the Deputy Speaker presiding has the Speaker's full powers with no appeal against his rulings; there is no mandatory rule about which party he comes from, and the Speaker does not move the motion
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the Rules of Procedure provide that the election of the Deputy Speaker is held on such date as the Speaker may fix. Statement 3 is correct — while presiding, the Deputy Speaker exercises all the powers of the Speaker and no appeal lies from his rulings to the Speaker. Statement 2 is wrong because the practice of offering the post to the opposition is only a convention; nothing makes it mandatory, and the office has often gone to the ruling side. Statement 4 is wrong because the Speaker presides over the House and does not himself move motions; the motion for the Deputy Speaker's election is moved and seconded by members.

items.value: Rice
items.reasoning: Flooded paddy fields are waterlogged and anaerobic, and the methanogenic archaea that thrive in that oxygen-free soil make rice cultivation the single largest agricultural source of methane. The same crop is also a major nitrous oxide source, because heavy nitrogenous fertiliser combined with the alternating wet and dry phases of the field drives both nitrification and denitrification, the two microbial pathways that release N2O. Cotton, sugarcane and wheat are grown on aerated soils and emit far less methane.

items.value: All three — SRI reduces seed requirement, methane production and electricity consumption
items.reasoning: SRI transplants single young seedlings at wide spacing instead of dense clumps, cutting seed rates by roughly an order of magnitude, so (1) holds. Alternate wetting and drying keeps the soil aerobic for much of the season, suppressing the methanogens that need waterlogged conditions, so (2) holds. Because the field is not kept continuously flooded, far less irrigation water is pumped, and where pumping is electric that directly lowers electricity use, so (3) holds. Marked MED because (3) is a second-order consequence that depends on irrigation being pump-fed rather than a property of the method itself.

items.value: Lake Faguibine
items.reasoning: Lake Faguibine in northern Mali, once one of the largest lakes in West Africa, dried out after the Sahelian droughts of the 1970s and 1980s and its bed is now largely sand and scrub. Lake Victoria is in East Africa and is the continent's largest lake by area; Lake Oguta in Nigeria is a small perennial lake that has not dried; and Lake Volta in Ghana is a large artificial reservoir behind the Akosombo Dam.

items.value: Pennar
items.reasoning: The Gandikota gorge in Kadapa district of Andhra Pradesh — often called the Grand Canyon of India — was cut by the Pennar (Penna) river through the Erramala hills, and the Gandikota fort stands on its rim. The Cauvery, Manjira and Tungabhadra all flow well away from this site, the Manjira and Tungabhadra being tributaries within the Godavari and Krishna systems respectively.

items.value: Only pair 2 is correct — Nanda Devi is in the Kumaon Himalaya; Namcha Barwa is not in the Garhwal Himalaya and Nokrek is not in the Sikkim Himalaya
items.reasoning: Pair 2 is correctly matched: Nanda Devi, the highest peak entirely within India, lies in Uttarakhand's Chamoli district in the Kumaon Himalaya. Pair 1 is wrong because Namcha Barwa stands at the eastern syntaxis where the Tsangpo turns south, in the Assam/eastern Himalaya, far from Garhwal. Pair 3 is wrong because Nokrek is the highest point of the Garo Hills in Meghalaya and a biosphere reserve there — it belongs to the Meghalaya plateau, not the Sikkim Himalaya.
